Phragmites and reed work

The catalogue distinguishes native and introduced reeds. It remembers phragmites used with cattails and bluestem grasses in dwelling coverings and mats, and describes food use in a gruel. It also emphasizes reeds’ relationships with soil, water, and wildlife.1

Elders described native reeds as important wetland plants that hold soil, shelter wildlife, and filter water before it reaches the bays.1

Places named in the catalogue

Long Island Sound; Shinnecock Bay; Heady Crick.1

Page references

The Shinnecock Environmental Department compiled this catalogue from elders’ memories and community resource knowledge in 2014. Food and medicine appear here as historical knowledge; safe identification and treatment require current guidance.

Shinnecock Environmental Department, Natural Resources Identified by Shinnecock Elders, April 4, 2014, PDF p. 8. Page numbers count the cover as PDF page 1.
